BHAWIKA CHHABRA/REUTERS BHAWIKA CHHABRA/REUTERS https://fl-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/bvwbom/article71626405.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/cjp-saurav-das-ranka.JPG BHAWIKA CHHABRA CJP-led protests demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation trigger a police crackdown, opposition mobilisation and renewed debate over electoral rights. CRACKDOWN ON CJP With the CJP’s call for the CEC’s resignation resonating across the nation, a rattled Central government seems determined to clamp down on the youth even as it goes easy on the political opposition. The controversy over alleged anomalies in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has been simmering for months, has now fuelled widespread protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over his alleged role in the mass deletion of crores of voter names from the rolls. https://frontline.thehindu.com/politics/gyanesh-kumar-row-modi-government-pressure/article71587343.ece Following back-to-back arrests of leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over protests in the national capital on the issue, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was granted conditional bail on October 17 after he submitted a peace bond with an undertaking to maintain peace without disrupting public order, while fellow CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to five days’ judicial custody on October 14. https://frontline.thehindu.com/columns/youth-protests-india-cockroach-movement-democracy-political-change/article71604254.ece Ranka and Das were arrested on October 14 while protesting against the government’s decision the day before to denotify Jantar Mantar as a protest site, while the police detained Dipke on October 16, hours before the CJP’s proposed Tiranga March at Connaught Place on the same day. On October 19, a special executive magistrate hearing Ranka and Das’ bail petition recused himself from the hearing, citing a threat to his life, while the CJP alleged that there was a deliberate delay in their release. The Delhi Police has registered a case over the threat. The CJP’s legal head, Ratna Singh, rued the fact that the four sureties submitted to secure their release had been rejected on “vague grounds”. The CJP posted on X: “Saurav and Ashutosh remain in judicial custody as their release plea goes unheard. There are deliberate delays, procedural irregularities, and a hearing derailed by an alleged threatening message instead of the merits of their release.” Their judicial custody got extended to two more days and hence they were released from jail only on October 21. Meanwhile, Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students’ Association, who has emerged as one of the most prominent faces of the protest, posted on X: “What should have been a bail hearing turned into a courtroom drama. A late entrance by the magistrate. A sudden, alleged threat as the plot twist. And the bail plea of Saurav & Ashutosh written out of the script. As if the ending was written before the curtains went up.” The AISA chief, however, challenged the Rs.10,000 peace bond notice in the Delhi High Court, saying that regime change is democratic, but the court on October 23 rejected her plea and asked her to furnish a personal bond of Rs.10,000 and one surety to maintain peace during inquiry. When protests gathered momentum Although protests on the SIR issue have been going on for months across the country, they gained momentum in Delhi in October, starting with a massive protest at Jantar Mantar on October 2 in which members of various parties’ student bodies took part. The same day, Dipke and others, backed by the actor Naseeruddin Shah, the singer Vishal Dadlani, and the activist Tushar Gandhi, called for a “jail bharo andolan” (fill the jails movement) at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. The Mumbai Police, which had denied permission for the gathering, detained protesters in large numbers. On October 6, the INDIA bloc organised a major protest in Delhi with Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi at the forefront; they followed it up with another protest on October 7. center Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, along with the INDIA bloc leaders, speaking to mediapersons on the SIR issue in New Delhi on October 13. NAVEEN SHARMA/ANI NAVEEN SHARMA/ANI https://fl-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/pwe5rv/article71626422.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/rahul-gandhi-sir.jpg Naveen Sharma CJP leaders face arrests and detention as protests against alleged voter deletions under the Special Intensive Revision spread across India. In both events, many leaders from other opposition parties took part. On October 10, Delhi went into a virtual lockdown, with 57 metro stations closed and several trains cancelled to prevent the CJP’s protests. Over 400 protesters were detained. The government’s actions drew sharp comments from the Supreme Court, which cautioned it against using a “hammer to kill a fly” in its security preparations to counter the proposed CJP protest. After being taken into custody, Dipke said that even Indira Gandhi did not take such measures during the Emergency. He said: “This is dictatorship. You can see where the nation is heading. They [Delhi Police] are here to arrest us directly from the flight. We are not afraid of getting arrested.…” Before boarding the flight to New Delhi, he had posted on X: “Modi has accepted defeat even before our protest has begun. The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength, but of a leader terrified of his own people.” The YouTuber and social influencer Dhruv Rathee was taken into preventive custody from his home in Gurugram, while Ratna Singh was also detained. The INDIA bloc’s protest on October 12 saw a massive surge in Delhi as protesters marched from the Constitution Club to the Supreme Court. The bloc is planning to organise a “maha rally” at the Ramlila Maidan on November 1. Reports from different State capitals suggested that the opposition is sensing a build-up of public sentiment against the government on this issue. On October 14, Rahul Gandhi posted on X: “The day is coming when those who seek to silence the voice of our democracy will face the harsh hand of justice. Be it Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Gyanesh Kumar, or any common foot soldier. I want every student and youth who has endured police brutality or unlawful detention to keep a complete record of it—videos or photos—these will be essential. Peaceful protest is your right. We will not allow anyone to snatch it away.” On October 17, BJP president Nitin Nabin hit out at the opposition, accusing it of “trying to destabilise the nation at the behest of foreign powers” and of not respecting the people’s mandate for the BJP, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He alleged that the opposition’s fight was not for electoral reforms, the SIR, or the future of the country’s youth but rather to spread anarchy in the country and seize power at any cost. He added that the government would fight it out firmly. The protests also echoed overseas, with Dhruv Rathee organising a protest in London. The government’s decision to clamp down heavily on the CJP protest resulted in senior politicians from different parties hitting the streets of Delhi and leaders such as former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, now heading a Trinamool Congress faction, the AAP’s Arvind Kejriwal, and the CPI(M) leaders Pinarayi Vijayan and Manik Sarkar courting arrest, along with a large number of Congress leaders led by Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi, and Priyanka Gandhi. Others detained included CPI(M) general secretary M.A. Baby, the party’s Rajya Sabha member Brinda Karat, Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation general secretary Dipankar, and the senior advocate Prashant Bhushan. A disturbing aspect of the protests was the sight of some right-wing activists and saffron-clad men doing their own policing, which the authorities ignored. One protester, wearing a “Hanuman Seva Dal Delhi” T-shirt, was seen dragging a young protester and handing him over to the Delhi Police. On October 6, Rahul Gandhi, who stood atop a barricade, said that the SIR was treason, while the Samajwadi Party accused the Election Commission of India (ECI) of targeting the “Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak” (Backward-Dalit-Minority) communities and creating a scenario in which only BJP supporters could vote. The protests were reminiscent of the opposition parties’ 2024 general election campaign when they had raised the battle cry that the Constitution was in danger, alleging that the BJP, if voted to power, could undermine the constitutional rights of reservation given to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes. center At the “Tiranga March” held in New Delhi against CEC Gyanesh Kumar on October 15. SUSHIL KUMAR VERMA SUSHIL KUMAR VERMA https://fl-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/p5ctuf/article71626479.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/tiranga-march-cec.jpg SUSHIL KUMAR VERMA Protests against SIR voter deletions expose political divisions over electoral rights, police powers and the treatment of dissent in India. A notable feature of the latest protests was Naveen Patnaik’s Biju Janata Dal (BJD) joining the protest in solidarity after a gap of several years during which it had kept an equal distance from the BJP and the Congress. The first sign of the BJD and the Congress coming closer had become visible during the Rajya Sabha election in Odisha in March this year, when they agreed to back a common candidate. Similarly, a notable absence from the protest was that of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which has been sulking ever since the Congress joined hands with its arch rival, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), in Tamil Nadu after the Assembly election results in May. The AAP, which initially did not participate in the INDIA bloc’s protest, later sent its representatives. The Congress will be taking on the AAP in the upcoming Assembly election in Punjab early next year. There were sporadic protests in all southern States and Puducherry demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation in response to the nationwide call by the Congress and the CJP. While the Congress-led or Congress-ruled States of Keralam, Karnataka, and Telangana approached the protest in different ways, the parties running Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Puducherry refused to have anything to do with it. Keralam went a step further, passing a resolution seeking the removal of the CEC. In Karnataka, people from various walks of life joined the protests in Bengaluru, Mangaluru, Kalaburagi, Vijayapura, Belagavi, Hassan, and other districts on both October 10 and October 12. The Bengaluru Police detained over 100 protesters when they attempted to march towards the office of the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer on October 12. Interestingly, in Tamil Nadu, the TVK did not organise protests nor did it participate in the Congress-led protests. The DMK took the lead in condemning the police action in both Tamil Nadu and Delhi and said that the “scale of repression being unleashed against peaceful protesters brings back painful memories of the Emergency”. In Telangana, the protests were widespread. The Bharat Rashtra Samithi protested on a different note, alleging that government officials loyal to the Congress had systematically removed its supporters from the electoral rolls, and demanded an inquiry by a sitting Supreme Court judge. In Andhra Pradesh, the ruling coalition, which the BJP is a part of, defended the CEC but allowed the opposition to organise protests. In Puducherry too, political parties followed the Andhra Pradesh model: the ruling All India N.R. Congress, which is in alliance with the BJP, has said nothing about the ECI or the demand that the CEC must resign. The Congress-led alliance held protests that leaders described as low-key. In Maharashtra, the Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena (UBT) organised a mass protest at Shivaji Park demanding the CEC’s resignation. Initially, during the protest against the NEET question paper leaks, Uddhav Thackeray actively supported the CJP and even travelled to Delhi to express solidarity with the activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was on a hunger strike. The protest provided Mamata Banerjee with a much-needed platform to regain political relevance after her defeat in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly election and the subsequent split in her party. After courting arrest in Delhi, she tried to organise a march in Kolkata on October 13 against the CEC, but the police halted it citing lack of permission. The actions against Dipke, Ranka, and Das clearly indicate that the Central government is determined to deal with the CJP with an iron hand even as it might provide some space to the mainstream opposition parties in the campaign against the ECI. With inputs from Vedaant Lakhera in New Delhi, R.K. Radhakrishnan in Chennai, Amey Tirodkar in Mumbai, and Suhrid Sankar Chattopadhyay in Kolkata.
